section_summary: This section begins with 1932–1934 investigations of allegations that Japanese residents were surveying Cuba, buying land near the Bay of Pigs for a possible aviation or naval base, or participating in political agitation; American diplomatic and military investigators found little or no supporting evidence. Most of the section concerns the 1937 arrest of George Yukichi Ozawa in Havana, where he had represented himself as a physician, Japanese naval officer, and legation associate, prompting investigations into illegal medical practice, fraud, narcotics violations, espionage, nationality, and his prior activities in the United States. Embassy reports, Cuban and American correspondence, identification records, photographs, and extensive press clippings document the inquiry, which failed to substantiate his medical credentials or locate an additional FBI record and led Cuban officials to recommend deportation.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on reported Japanese surveying and fishing activities in Cuba
subfiles.from: Hayne Ellis, Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.to: H. Freeman Matthews, Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards allegations that 2,000 Japanese fishermen were actually conducting naval surveys along Cuba's southern coast.
subfiles.summary: Ellis quotes a reserve officer's September 23, 1930 letter alleging that Japanese residents ostensibly engaged in fishing were sounding and surveying from Santa Clara Province to Cape San Antonio. The source placed their headquarters on O'Reilly Street in Havana and said they also met on Avenida 10 de Octubre in La Víbora. Naval Intelligence requested further information because it had no naval attaché in Cuba.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 516 concerning Japanese property near Cochinos Bay
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.to: Harry F. Guggenheim, American Ambassador at Havana
subfiles.about: Directs the Embassy to investigate reported Japanese property purchases near the Bay of Pigs and their possible use as an aviation base.
subfiles.summary: The Department asks whether Japanese purchasers had acquired property on the bay's western shore and, if so, for what purpose. It repeats the earlier naval allegation about Japanese fishermen surveying southern Cuba and maintaining meeting places in Havana. The possibility that the property could support an aviation base made the inquiry important.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Walter Wilcox
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Records Wilcox's claim that Japanese buyers were acquiring land across a southern Cuban bay from his property.
subfiles.summary: Wilcox used a map to identify his own land and the tract he believed Japanese interests were purchasing across the bay. He warned that the location might be developed as a base for an attack on the Panama Canal.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1109, Japanese Activities in Cuba
subfiles.from: Harry F. Guggenheim, American Embassy at Havana
subfiles.about: Reports Embassy findings on Japanese residents, fishermen, and alleged property acquisition near the Bay of Pigs.
subfiles.summary: Corroborating Japanese and Cuban official sources placed Cuba's Japanese population at about 700, including farmers on the Isle of Pines and roughly sixty fishermen operating from Cienfuegos. The Embassy found no confirmation that Japanese interests had acquired property near the bay, whose swampy shores were sparsely inhabited and poorly suited to settlement. A definitive title search or ground inquiry would require funds and personnel the Embassy lacked, although the ambassador intended to revisit the district. He also cautioned that Caribbean claims about Japanese colonization sometimes exploited American anxieties.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note on Havana Despatch No. 1317
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes the ambassador's failure to find a Japanese settlement near the Bay of Pigs.
subfiles.summary: The note records that the ambassador visited the relevant area of Cuba. Contrary to the reported Japanese property purchases, he found no indication or evidence of a Japanese settlement on the bay's western shore.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1317, Japanese Activities in Cuba
subfiles.from: Harry F. Guggenheim, American Embassy at Havana
subfiles.about: Reports the ambassador's personal visit to the Bay of Pigs area and rejection of the settlement allegation.
subfiles.summary: Guggenheim refers to his earlier Despatch No. 1109 and reports visiting the district during the preceding weekend. Although he could not conduct an exhaustive investigation, neither his observations nor his inquiries revealed the slightest evidence of a Japanese settlement.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division distribution sheet
subfiles.from: Military Intelligence Division, War Department
subfiles.to: Department of State and listed military offices
subfiles.about: Routes military intelligence material concerning Japanese activities in Cuba for information or filing.
subfiles.summary: The sheet lists War Department, service-school, Navy, State, and Commerce recipients. Its markings show circulation to the State Department's Latin American and Far Eastern divisions.

subfiles.title: Memorandum: Activities of Japanese agents in Cuba
subfiles.from: C. A. Lynch, Headquarters Second Corps Area
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: Condenses Winston Ehrgott's allegations that Japanese agents were agitating Cuban workers after the Grau government took power.
subfiles.summary: Ehrgott claimed that about 250 Japanese were active in provincial districts, sometimes working with Communist or other radical agitators, although he did not describe them as Communist Party members. The memorandum explicitly notes that his account lacked definite facts or collateral confirmation.

subfiles.title: Military Attaché memorandum rejecting Ehrgott's allegations
subfiles.from: T. N. Gimperling, Military Attaché at Havana
subfiles.about: Finds no foundation for claims that Japanese residents participated in subversive activity against the Grau government.
subfiles.summary: Gimperling reports that investigations found no Japanese involvement in labor agitation or political subversion, while other nationalities had been identified in such activity. Major Tabernilla stated that no Japanese had been arrested or suspected, and most of Cuba's roughly 700 Japanese residents were farmers. Gimperling characterizes Ehrgott as an opportunist and troublemaker whose influence with Grau had collapsed, and describes his unsuccessful proposal that Batista employ him and several lightly trained Americans as Cuban Army instructors.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 8171, Arrest of Yukihi George Ozawa
subfiles.from: H. Freeman Matthews, American Embassy at Havana
subfiles.about: Reports Ozawa's arrest and the conflicting claims surrounding his identity, medical practice, debts, and possible espionage.
subfiles.summary: Ozawa was arrested on February 8 amid suspicions of narcotics activity and complaints that he obtained goods on credit by claiming Japanese diplomatic or naval status. Although he had treated patients at the Anglo-American Hospital and attended the injured daughter of Japanese Chargé Takaharu Ito, the Japanese Legation denied that he was a Japanese subject, attaché, or naval doctor. Hospital chairman Clifford Henry Stapleton described unpaid bills and doubts about Ozawa's qualifications. The despatch encloses photographs and three press reports.

subfiles.title: Photographs of Ozawa from Diario de la Marina
subfiles.from: Diario de la Marina
subfiles.about: Provides three press photographs associated with the report that Ozawa posed as a Japanese naval officer.
subfiles.summary: The surviving OCR contains the enclosure heading and a caption identifying Ozawa as an officer of the Japanese navy. The photographs themselves were enclosed with Embassy Despatch No. 8171.

subfiles.title: “Un extraño japonés” — Diario de la Marina report on Ozawa's arrest
subfiles.from: Diario de la Marina
subfiles.about: Describes Ozawa's arrest, alleged impersonation of a naval physician and attaché, and the documents and equipment seized from him.
subfiles.summary: Merchant Leonardo Naredo Venta complained that Ozawa obtained merchandise on credit while posing as a Japanese naval doctor and diplomatic attaché. Police linked him to visits aboard foreign ships and seized maps, medical instruments, uniforms, official papers, photographs of Batista and American soldiers, and other materials that fueled espionage suspicions. Ozawa reportedly remained silent under questioning, while the authorities investigated illegal medical practice, fraud, and possible spying.

subfiles.title: “Japanese Legation Here Denies Ozawa is Citizen”
subfiles.from: Havana Post
subfiles.about: Reports the Japanese Legation's denial that Ozawa was Japanese or officially connected with it and summarizes the police investigation.
subfiles.summary: The article states that Ozawa was detained while leaving the S.S. Rotterdam and was initially suspected of drug smuggling before maps, uniforms, coded cables, debts, and inconsistent statements prompted espionage suspicions. It notes planned travel through New York to Bremen and possible immigration and illegal-practice charges. A statement signed by T. Okura says the Legation knew Ozawa socially but believed from his own assertions that he was American-born and medically qualified, while denying that he held any official post.

subfiles.title: El País report on Ozawa's patients and the Japanese Legation's denial
subfiles.from: El País
subfiles.about: Lists patients treated by Ozawa, recounts his access to the Anglo-American Hospital, and reproduces the Japanese Legation's statement.
subfiles.summary: Hospital officials Clifford Henry Stapleton and Carlos Deschapelles said Ozawa admitted patients while they believed he was a Japanese naval physician, but excluded him after learning that he was not registered with the Cuban health authorities. The article lists numerous patients, including the Japanese minister's daughter and Charles Baughn, whose deaths received special attention. It also describes recommendation letters connected with the Haitian Legation and Shinobu Sekihara, while reproducing T. Okura's denial of Ozawa's Japanese citizenship or official status.

subfiles.title: Instruction transmitting Pennsylvania correspondence on Ozawa
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards copies of Pennsylvania correspondence and the Department's reply concerning Ozawa.
subfiles.summary: The Department refers to Despatch No. 8171 and later reports about Ozawa's arrest. It transmits a March 4 letter and enclosures from Pennsylvania Deputy Attorney General Edward Friedman, together with a copy of the Department's response to the governor.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 8178, Arrest of Yukihi George Ozawa
subfiles.from: H. Freeman Matthews, American Embassy at Havana
subfiles.about: Reports Ozawa's expected indictment for illegally practicing medicine and planned investigation of two patient deaths.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reports that Ozawa was scheduled for indictment before Havana's Fourth Instructional Court. His arrival in Cuba in February 1935, his claim to be a Japanese Embassy attaché, uncertain American birth, and contradictory background statements were under investigation. Authorities also intended to examine the deaths of Haruko Ito and Charles R. Baughn at the Anglo-American Hospital.

subfiles.title: “El Servicio Secreto norteamericano actúa para determinar la personalidad”
subfiles.from: Diario de la Marina
subfiles.about: Reports efforts to establish whether Ozawa was a fantasist, opportunist, or spy and reconstructs his arrival in Cuba.
subfiles.summary: The article says Ozawa would be prosecuted for illegal medical practice and describes competing claims that he was born in Los Angeles to Japanese and American parents. It reports that he traveled to Havana as “Reginald Osana,” represented himself as connected to the Japanese Embassy, cultivated Japanese, civil, and military contacts, and wore a naval-style uniform. Cuban police and American authorities were attempting to establish his identity.

subfiles.title: “Ozawa Unlisted on Sanitation Bureau Record”
subfiles.from: Havana Post
subfiles.about: Reports that Ozawa was not registered as a physician and that two patient deaths were under review.
subfiles.summary: Sanitation records showed no physician registration for Ozawa. Officials examined the death certificates of Haruko Ito and Charles R. Baughn, signed respectively by Dr. Sigarroa and Carlos Deschapelles, and expected Ozawa's indictment and arraignment.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 8186, Ozawa indicted for alleged illegal practice of medicine
subfiles.from: H. Freeman Matthews, American Embassy at Havana
subfiles.about: Reports Ozawa's indictment, efforts to establish his identity, and the continuing military-information inquiry.
subfiles.summary: Ozawa was indicted on February 13, with bail fixed at 500 pesos, and Cuban authorities requested American assistance in determining his identity. In a jail interview he claimed birth in Japan to an English mother and Japanese father and asserted that he held a University of California medical degree, while denying that he practiced medicine in Cuba. Cuban military authorities continued investigating whether he collected military information.

subfiles.title: “Ozawa Indicted by Cuban Court”
subfiles.from: Havana Post
subfiles.about: Reports Ozawa's indictment for illegal medical practice and the request for United States help identifying him.
subfiles.summary: The article reviews Ozawa's arrest after leaving the Rotterdam, the Japanese Legation's denial, and the discovery of debts and unlicensed medical activity. It states that police believed Japanese cruiser officers knew him as a naval officer, although the Legation denied any naval connection. Dr. Luis Castellanos requested an American report on Ozawa's identity.

subfiles.title: El País jail interview with George Ozawa
subfiles.from: El País
subfiles.about: Presents Ozawa's account of his origins, education, medical activities, arrival in Cuba, and denial of espionage.
subfiles.summary: Interviewed through Miguel Cortés, Ozawa claimed Japanese birth, an English mother, education at the universities of California and Virginia, and medical work in the United States. He said advice received in New Orleans led him to Cuba in February 1935, where he merely observed operations at the Anglo-American Hospital rather than practiced medicine. He denied being a spy, defended his uniform as a club uniform, and promised to produce credentials, while the article recounted his financial problems and involvement in the cases of the Japanese minister's daughter and another patient.

subfiles.title: True copy of Despatch No. 8186
subfiles.from: H. Freeman Matthews, American Embassy at Havana
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy reporting Ozawa's indictment and the investigation into his identity and possible collection of military information.
subfiles.summary: This true copy repeats the report that Ozawa was indicted for illegal medical practice with bail set at 500 pesos. It also repeats his claims of Japanese birth and a University of California degree and notes the Cuban military inquiry into possible intelligence collection.

subfiles.title: Duplicate clipping: “Ozawa Indicted by Cuban Court”
subfiles.from: Havana Post
subfiles.about: Duplicate press report of Ozawa's indictment and the attempt to determine his nationality.
subfiles.summary: The clipping repeats that Ozawa was indicted for practicing medicine illegally and that the Japanese Legation denied his nationality and official status. It also recounts his arrest, debts, alleged naval connections, and the request to United States authorities for identifying information.

subfiles.title: Faded duplicate of Despatch No. 8186
subfiles.from: H. Freeman Matthews, American Embassy at Havana
subfiles.about: Poorly reproduced duplicate of the report on Ozawa's indictment and suspected intelligence activity.
subfiles.summary: Despite severely degraded OCR, the text is another copy of Despatch No. 8186. It reports the illegal-practice indictment, American assistance sought for identification, Ozawa's biographical claims, and the continuing military inquiry.

subfiles.title: Second faded duplicate of Despatch No. 8186
subfiles.from: H. Freeman Matthews, American Embassy at Havana
subfiles.about: Another degraded record copy of the Embassy's February 15 report on Ozawa.
subfiles.summary: The document repeats the indictment, 500-peso bail, and Cuban request for United States help establishing Ozawa's identity. It again notes his claimed medical degree and the investigation of possible military-information collection.

subfiles.title: Third faded duplicate of Despatch No. 8186
subfiles.from: H. Freeman Matthews, American Embassy at Havana
subfiles.about: Additional degraded duplicate concerning Ozawa's indictment, identity, and possible espionage.
subfiles.summary: This copy again records Ozawa's indictment and the request for an American identity report. It repeats his account of Japanese birth and California medical education and the Cuban military authorities' continuing suspicions.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 8205, Further data regarding Yukihi George Ozawa
subfiles.from: H. Freeman Matthews, American Embassy at Havana
subfiles.about: Transmits further press reporting on Ozawa's case and comments on the weakness of the espionage allegation.
subfiles.summary: The despatch notes Ozawa's illegal-practice indictment and a separate fraud suit brought by the Plaza Hotel. Cuban officials awaited an identity report from the “Secret Service in Washington,” while the press continued emphasizing espionage without convincing evidence. American physician H. P. A. Taylor privately described Ozawa as a possible mental case and doubted that he possessed a medical degree.

subfiles.title: Diario de la Marina report on maps seized from Ozawa
subfiles.from: Diario de la Marina
subfiles.about: Reports police suspicions arising from maps, photographs, uniforms, passes, and other items seized from Ozawa.
subfiles.summary: Police emphasized Ozawa's prolonged stay as a tourist, his naval uniform, official contacts, and maps of La Víbora and an unidentified port thought to be Cuban. Photographs of American soldiers and passes permitting entry to foreign ships further encouraged the spy theory. The article also discusses the deaths of Maruka Ito and Charles Boughn, the Plaza Hotel fraud case, Ozawa's change of defense counsel, and the awaited American identity report.

subfiles.title: Pennsylvania Department of Justice letter forwarding Ozawa records
subfiles.from: Edward Friedman, Deputy Attorney General of Pennsylvania
subfiles.about: Asks whether Pennsylvania may send Cuban authorities its police information about George Ozawa.
subfiles.summary: Friedman encloses a letter from Israel Castellanos requesting an investigation of Ozawa and a Pennsylvania State Police report on the subject. He asks whether the State Department objects to forwarding the information to Castellanos. Pages 48–49 are partial or duplicate reproductions of the cover letter.

subfiles.title: Pennsylvania State Police report concerning George Ozawa
subfiles.from: Pennsylvania State Police
subfiles.about: Provides investigative information on Ozawa's prior activities in Pennsylvania.
subfiles.summary: The cover letter identifies these pages as an enclosed Pennsylvania State Police report concerning Ozawa. The surviving OCR is almost entirely illegible, and page 51 contains no readable text, so its specific findings cannot be recovered from this section.

subfiles.title: Request for investigation of George W. Ozawa
subfiles.from: Israel Castellanos, Cuban National Identification Bureau
subfiles.to: Superintendent, Pennsylvania State Bureau of Identification
subfiles.about: Requests fingerprint and field investigation of Ozawa's Pennsylvania residence, medical claims, and possible espionage.
subfiles.summary: Castellanos forwards fingerprints, photographs, and a motor-vehicle registration record and asks Pennsylvania to trace Ozawa's record and activities. Cuban evidence showed that he wore a Japanese naval uniform, associated with the Japanese colony and Legation, and practiced medicine without producing credentials. The letter asks investigators to contact the Memorial Hospital in Johnstown and medical institutions and states that Cuban authorities suspected him of being an international spy.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to the Governor of Pennsylvania
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Approves Pennsylvania's release of information about Ozawa to Israel Castellanos.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Edward Friedman's March 4 communication and states that it has no objection to Pennsylvania furnishing the requested information. It informs the governor that Ozawa had been indicted in Havana on February 13 for illegal medical practice. Copies were being sent to the American Embassy in Havana, and Friedman's enclosures were returned.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 8319, Case of Yukihi George Ozawa
subfiles.from: H. Freeman Matthews, American Embassy at Havana
subfiles.about: Transmits a press translation of Israel Castellanos's report on American inquiries into Ozawa's background.
subfiles.summary: The report indicated that Ozawa may have been born in San Francisco and had disappeared from there ten years earlier. Investigators found no proof of a medical degree. The Cuban National Identification Bureau recommended his deportation.

subfiles.title: “What Happened to Ozawa During Past Ten Years?”
subfiles.from: Havana Post
subfiles.about: Publishes the principal findings of Castellanos's identity investigation and recommendation that Ozawa be deported.
subfiles.summary: Castellanos reported that Ozawa was a son of San Francisco broker Aizo Ozawa and disappeared while studying civil engineering about ten years earlier. Albany institutions, state medical authorities, professional directories, and the Pan-American Medical Association had no record of his medical training or practice. The report characterized him as a charlatan who had illegally treated varied patients, found his activities suspicious socially and internationally, and recommended deportation as dangerous and undesirable.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 8411, Yukihi George Ozawa
subfiles.from: H. Freeman Matthews, American Embassy at Havana
subfiles.about: Forwards Cuban identification circulars bearing Ozawa's photograph, fingerprints, and description.
subfiles.summary: Ozawa remained detained on charges including narcotics violations and illegal medical practice. The Embassy enclosed two copies of a National Identification Bureau circular requesting information about him. The circulars included his fingerprints, photograph, and physical description.

subfiles.title: Governor Earle's acknowledgment of State Department approval
subfiles.from: George H. Earle, Governor of Pennsylvania
subfiles.about: Acknowledges approval of Pennsylvania's cooperation with Cuba in the Ozawa investigation.
subfiles.summary: Earle thanks Hull for the March 11 letter concerning Edward Friedman's correspondence and Israel Castellanos's request. He expresses satisfaction that the Pennsylvania Department of Justice's action met with State Department approval.

subfiles.title: Attorney General's report on the FBI record search for Ozawa
subfiles.from: Attorney General of the United States
subfiles.about: Reports that FBI files contained no additional record concerning Ozawa.
subfiles.summary: The Attorney General acknowledges receipt of the Embassy communication and duplicate Cuban fingerprint circulars. The FBI Identification Division found no Ozawa record beyond the material already supplied by the State Department and had notified Cuban police of that result on March 10.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding the Attorney General's Ozawa letter
subfiles.from: Secretary of State
subfiles.to: American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim at Havana
subfiles.about: Transmits the Attorney General's April 19 report that the FBI found no additional record for Ozawa.
subfiles.summary: The Department refers to the Embassy's April 17 despatch and earlier correspondence concerning Ozawa's prosecution in Cuba. It encloses a copy of the Attorney General's April 19 letter for the Embassy's information.
